report:
**Conclusion: no.** High-quality randomized-trial evidence does not show that hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) reduces death from COVID-19.

* The large RECOVERY randomized trial in hospitalized patients found **28-day mortality was 26.8% with HCQ versus 25.0% with usual care** (rate ratio 1.09; 95% CI 0.97–1.23). Thus, results excluded a meaningful mortality benefit and were compatible with modest harm. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926  
* A Cochrane systematic review concluded HCQ has **no useful effect for treating COVID-19** and that further treatment trials were not warranted based on the accumulated evidence. https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013587_chloroquine-or-hydroxychloroquine-useful-treating-people-covid-19-or-preventing-infection-people-who  
* The NIH’s randomized ORCHID trial likewise concluded HCQ provided **no clinical benefit** in hospitalized adults. https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/hydroxychloroquine-does-not-benefit-adults-hospitalized-covid-19  
* HCQ also did not establish preventive benefit; WHO made a **strong recommendation against** its use to prevent COVID-19. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-2019-nCoV-prophylaxes-2023.1  

Why the earlier “yes” impression arose: some early observational studies reported better outcomes, but treated and untreated groups can differ in illness severity, timing of care, and other treatments. Random assignment is designed to address those biases, and the large randomized evidence did not confirm a survival benefit. HCQ can also cause adverse effects, including potentially serious heart-rhythm problems, so it should not be used for COVID-19 outside an appropriate clinician-directed context.
